app.tagline: Hand a list to someone standing next to you — no internet needed.

chapter.heading: What this chapter is for
chapter.goal: A tutorial chapter — the fifth. Each one adds a single idea to the one before it; this one takes the internet away. Two devices that have never met, no server, no relay, nothing arranging the introduction: somebody holds up a code, somebody else scans it, and a list crosses.

connection.label: The connection
connection.text: A WebRTC session negotiated from a code held up to a camera, with nothing in the middle to arrange it.

identity.label: Your signature
identity.text: A passkey becomes a DID. An Ed25519 key, encrypted where it rests, signs your entries after a single prompt per session.

varsig.label: Present, and deliberately off
varsig.text: The stricter variant asks for the passkey on every single write. It ships with the identity provider, and this chapter does not switch it on — which is why it appears in the lockfile and nowhere in the code.

permissions.label: Who may write
permissions.text: A list is opened with write access for its owner alone. The other side replicates it and reads it, and cannot add a line.

database.label: The list itself
database.text: A keyvalue store whose address is the hash of its own manifest. That is what makes an address impossible to guess, and therefore worth handing over.

storage.label: Where it survives
storage.text: Blocks and index live in this browser's IndexedDB. With no relay to fetch them back from, they have to be on the device or the list is gone at the next reload.

protocol.label: The handover
protocol.text: This app's own protocol, carrying versioned JSON envelopes dispatched on a kind field — so the list offer and everything after it share one stream instead of earning a protocol each.

relay.label: Optional, and off
relay.text: A directory lookup that finds a relay when the addresses baked into the build have rotated away. Nothing contacts it unless the box above is ticked.

simple.whatItIs: A to-do list you can hand to somebody else. No server, no account — it goes from your device to theirs and lives in both browsers.
simple.lead: Hold up your code, they scan it, then they hold up their answer and you scan back. No internet needed for that, but both devices have to be on the same network — otherwise one opens a hotspot and the other joins it.
simple.passkey: A passkey is your signature: it shows the other side the entries came from you. The app works without one.

tech.heading: Why it sometimes fails on a mobile network
tech.nat: Mobile networks commonly use symmetric NAT, which defeats exactly the direct connection the code sets up.
tech.chromeIpv6: Chrome does not surface IPv6 WebRTC candidates, so the path that would otherwise work on a mobile network is not offered at all.
tech.browsers: DuckDuckGo, Safari, Firefox and others appear to pass IPv6 candidates reliably. One caveat: DuckDuckGo may not support passkeys on Android or GrapheneOS.
tech.graphene: Vanadium on GrapheneOS works well with WebRTC enabled in the security settings — and, if you use passkeys, Passchain from Accrescent installed.
tech.vpn: If both devices are on mobile data, a VPN such as NymVPN gets you past the NAT.

check.heading: This device, right now
check.none: Your network offers no path out over IPv4 or IPv6.
check.sameNetwork: If you are on the same Wi-Fi or hotspot as the other device, none of this matters and it works anyway.
check.routable: Your network allows a direct connection even to devices on other networks.
check.localOnly: Your network assigns a new port per destination (symmetric NAT). That will not reach a device on another network.

relay.hint: Off by default: this app needs no server. Tick it only if the other device cannot scan your code — over a messenger, for instance.

ways.heading: How the other device gets in
ways.qr: By camera: you hold up a code, they scan it. Nothing leaves this network.
ways.qrWithRelay: By camera: you hold up a code, they scan it. Nothing leaves this network. A relay answered, so the other device can also join without a code.

privacy.heading: What this means for your data
privacy.empty: The choices above decide what goes here.
privacy.accept: I have read this and accept it
privacy.noServer: We run no server, and no copy of your list exists anywhere we control.
privacy.qr: A code carried from this screen to the other device. The list goes straight from one to the other and leaves this network only if you send the link.
privacy.relayOn: A relay introduces the two devices to each other. It may hold data briefly so the other device can collect it after this one goes offline.
privacy.relayOff: No relay is contacted. Without one, the other device has to be reachable from this network.
privacy.passkey: Your passkey signs what you write, so the other side can see the entries came from you. It stays on this device.
privacy.throwaway: A temporary key for this browser signs your entries. Nobody can attribute them to you, and it is gone when you clear this browser.
privacy.local: Your lists live in this browser. Clearing it clears them.
privacy.gateway: The app itself is delivered through a public IPFS gateway, which sees that you loaded it. Running your own Kubo node, or the IPFS Companion extension, fetches it from the network instead — nobody in the middle, and it keeps working if a gateway is down.

warning.heading: Early days
warning.body: This is a working demonstration rather than a finished product. It does what it says, and the format may still change — so keep anything you would be sorry to lose somewhere else as well.
